opus-5.5.text:
I think text captures a surprising amount, but it captures the world at one remove. Text is what humans chose to write down, so next-token prediction learns the compressed residue of our reasoning, our explanations, our arguments. That's not nothing. If you predict the next token of a proof well enough, you have to model something about why the proof works, not just how it sounds.

But the gap I keep coming back to, especially from the math side, is that text rewards plausibility, not truth. A model can produce something that reads exactly like a correct argument, with all the right words in the right places, and still be wrong at step seven. In most domains you can't easily tell. Natural language has no built-in referee.

That's why I find mathematics such an interesting testbed. In math you can attach a verifier. If you write the argument in a formal language like Lean, the computer checks every step, and either it compiles or it doesn't. So you get a signal that isn't "does this look like what a human would write" but "is this actually correct." That changes the learning problem. You move from imitation toward something more like grounded search, where the model can try things, fail, get precise feedback, and improve beyond the distribution of what humans have already written.

So my view is roughly this. Next-token prediction on text gives you an extraordinary prior: intuition, analogy, the sense of which direction might be fruitful. That's a lot like a mathematician's taste. What it doesn't give you on its own is rigor, the ability to know when you're right. I think the interesting systems will combine the two: language models for intuition and exploration, and formal verification for truth. In math we're lucky that the second part can be made fully precise. In the physical world the verifier is experiment, which is slower and messier, but I think the principle is the same.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that next-token prediction captures far more of the world than most of us expected, and also something structurally less than the whole.

Here's how I think about it. Human text is a compressed record of how people reason, argue, prove, plan, and make mistakes. When you train a model to predict the next token across a huge chunk of that record, you're forcing it to build an internal model of whatever generated the text. For a lot of domains, that generator is human thought itself. So the model ends up learning a surprisingly rich approximation of concepts, causal stories, and the structure of arguments, not because anyone told it to, but because that's the cheapest way to get the prediction right.

Math is the domain I care most about, and it's a nice test case. A proof written in natural language is a trace of reasoning, and if you can predict the next step of a proof reliably, you've absorbed something real about mathematical structure. That's why these models can do things in math that would have sounded absurd a few years ago.

But there are at least two things text doesn't give you. First, text is a lossy projection of the world. People write down what's worth writing down, which means the obvious, the embodied, the physical, the stuff everyone already knows, is systematically underrepresented. Second, and this is the one I think matters more, text captures the outputs of reasoning much better than the process. When a mathematician publishes a proof, the dead ends, the wrong conjectures, the months of being stuck, none of that is in the paper. So a model trained on the clean record sees the answer and not the search.

That's why I don't think next-token prediction alone gets you to the frontier of knowledge. It gets you an extraordinary compression of what humanity has already written. To go past that, you need something that can actually search, verify, and get feedback from the world, whether that's a formal proof checker, an experiment, or a user who tells you you're wrong. The language model is the prior. The frontier comes from what you do on top of it.

astra-6.text:
I think text captures a remarkable amount of the world, but it’s still a projection of the world. People write about what they observe, what they believe, and how things work, so predicting that text well can require learning something about the underlying structure. If you’re trying to predict the next step in a mathematical proof, for example, understanding the mathematics is useful—you can’t always get there just by matching the surface form.

But I’d separate the training objective from what the model actually learns. Next-token prediction is an objective; it doesn’t tell us, by itself, whether the model has learned a robust abstraction or a shortcut that works in familiar contexts. Both can produce very convincing language.

And there are things that text leaves out. We have physical experiences and tacit knowledge that we don’t fully articulate. So I wouldn’t say that learning from text is merely learning about words, but I also wouldn’t assume that mastering text means understanding every aspect of the world. The interesting question is where those learned representations hold up when you put them in a genuinely new situation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think text captures a remarkable amount of the world, but it’s a very particular view of it. People write down observations, explanations, arguments, and discoveries, so predicting text well can require learning some of the structure behind those things. It’s more than learning which words tend to appear together.

But there’s a gap between the world and what people choose to say about it. A lot of physical intuition, practical knowledge, and everyday experience is left unstated. And text contains mistakes and contradictions, too. So I’d distinguish learning a model of how people describe the world from learning a model of the world itself. Those overlap substantially, but they’re not identical.

The interesting question to me is where prediction pushes a system to discover underlying structure, and where it can succeed by picking up patterns that don’t generalize beyond the text.
